opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most important distinctions in robotics right now, and people often blur the two.

On the reasoning side, which I'd call high-level planning or semantic understanding, progress has been dramatic, mostly thanks to large language models and vision-language models. A few years ago, if you asked a robot to "clean up the kitchen," it couldn't break that down. Now we can hand the problem to a foundation model and it will say: first pick up the cups, put them in the sink, wipe the counter, throw away the wrapper. It understands objects, context, even common-sense things like not putting a laptop in the dishwasher. That layer has basically ridden the wave of internet-scale pretraining, so it's improved almost for free.

The action side, the low-level control of actually executing those steps, is where things are much harder and slower. Knowing you should pick up the cup is very different from closing the gripper at the right place, with the right force, without knocking it over, on a cup you've never seen, under different lighting, on a different table. There's no internet of robot actions. All of that data has to be collected physically, by teleoperation or autonomous collection on real hardware, which is expensive and slow. So the action layer doesn't get the same scaling benefits.

One way I think about it: reasoning is now often not the bottleneck. If you look at where robots fail in real deployments, it's rarely because the plan was wrong. It's because the grasp slipped, or the robot couldn't recover from a small perturbation, or a contact-rich task like folding cloth or inserting a plug was simply beyond its dexterity. The brain has gotten ahead of the body, so to speak.

That's why a lot of the field is pushing toward end-to-end vision-language-action models, where the same network that reasons also outputs motor commands, in the hope that some of the semantic knowledge transfers into the physical skills. We've seen encouraging signs of that, like better generalization to new objects and instructions. But physical competence still largely scales with physical data, and figuring out how to get much more of it, whether through fleets, simulation, or human video, is in my view the central open problem.

r002.rationale: It credits large language and vision-language models and internet-scale pretraining, but does not identify general vision research as a source of transferable advances.

r003.rationale: It says reasoning benefited from internet-scale pretraining, but does not compare its scaling behavior with other modalities in large vision-language models.

r004.rationale: It says physical competence scales with physical data and calls obtaining more data an open problem, but does not state that action scaling laws are poorly understood.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the cleanest way to think about it is that reasoning and action live in very different data regimes, and that's really what separates how fast each one moves.

On the reasoning side, you have the entire internet. Language models get to learn from basically all of recorded human thought, so when you see a model plan out "I need to find the cup, pick it up, bring it to the sink," that capability is almost free now. It's inherited from the web. The semantic understanding, the task decomposition, the common sense about what objects are and how they relate to each other, all of that has been progressing on the same curve as the rest of the language model world. And honestly, robotics gets to ride that curve for free.

Action is a completely different story. There's no internet-scale dataset of robot trajectories. Every data point costs you real time, a real robot, usually a human operator, and the data is incredibly specific to the embodiment you collected it on. So the low-level question of "how do I actually move my gripper six centimeters to the left without knocking over the glass," that progress is bottlenecked on physical data collection, and it's been much slower and much more incremental.

So the way I'd actually measure the distinction is: if a robot fails, ask whether it failed because it didn't know what to do, or because it knew exactly what to do and couldn't execute it. A few years ago, failures were mostly the first kind. Now, overwhelmingly, failures are the second kind. The model will tell you a perfectly reasonable plan and then fumble the grasp. That shift in failure mode is, to me, the clearest evidence that reasoning has outrun action.

And the interesting thing is that these two are starting to get coupled. With the vision-language-action models, you're not treating planning and control as separate modules anymore. The hope is that the reasoning prior actually makes the action learning more sample efficient, because the model already understands what a mug is before it ever has to pick one up. Whether that fully closes the gap, I think, is still an open question, but it's definitely the bet a lot of the field is making right now.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says reasoning has outrun action and describes action progress as much slower and more incremental.

r002.rationale: It attributes reasoning gains to internet-scale language data, but does not identify general vision research as a source of transferable advances.

r003.rationale: It compares reasoning progress to the language-model curve, but does not say robotic reasoning scales like other modalities in large vision-language models.

r004.rationale: It describes physical data collection as an action bottleneck, but does not state that scaling laws for robotic action remain poorly understood.

r005.rationale: It does not discuss how close different parts of robotics are to commercialization.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to separate reasoning about what to do from actually being able to do it. A model might look at a kitchen and say, “To make coffee, I need to pick up the cup, put it under the machine, and press the button.” That’s a sensible plan. But picking up the cup requires understanding its geometry, making contact, applying the right force, and adjusting if it slips. Having the plan doesn’t automatically give you those capabilities.

So progress in reasoning is about handling more complex goals, breaking them into steps, and recognizing when a plan needs to change. Progress in action is about how reliably you can execute those steps across different objects and environments.

And they interact. If the robot fails to grasp the cup, it needs to notice that and decide whether to try again or change its approach. The key question is whether its reasoning stays connected to what it can actually perceive and do. In robotics, a good explanation of the task is only part of the story; you also need the task to succeed in the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes planning from execution but does not say action capabilities are progressing more slowly than reasoning.

r002.rationale: It does not identify general vision research as a source of advances for robotic reasoning.

r003.rationale: It discusses more complex goals and plans, but does not describe reasoning as scaling like other modalities in large vision-language models.

r004.rationale: It does not address whether scaling laws for robotic action capabilities are understood.

r005.rationale: It does not compare robotics areas by their proximity to commercialization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful to separate knowing what to do from being able to do it. A model might reason correctly that, to clear a table, it should pick up a cup and put it in the sink. But that doesn’t tell you whether the robot can grasp that particular cup, handle it being slippery, or recover if it moves unexpectedly.

So I would measure reasoning progress by the quality of the decisions: can the system understand the task, break it down, and choose an appropriate next step? And I would measure action progress by what happens when it actually interacts with the world: how reliably can it execute, across different objects and environments?

Of course, those two things are coupled. An action changes what you observe, and that observation should change your plan. The important question is whether better reasoning translates into better task completion on a physical robot. You can have a very compelling explanation of a plan and still fail at the first grasp.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes reasoning from physical execution but does not say that action capabilities are progressing more slowly.

r004.rationale: It says reasoning may not translate into task completion, but does not state that scaling laws for robotic actions are poorly understood.
